title: Knowing When It’s Time to Quit
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article reframes strategic quitting as a leadership skill rather than a failure, distinguishing it from reactive quitting driven by emotional withdrawal. Drawing on decision-making expert Annie Duke's concept of "kill criteria," the piece recommends setting clear, predetermined checkpoints — deadlines, benchmarks, cost thresholds — before launching any strategy, so that the decision to walk away is triggered by data rather than in-the-moment sunk-cost thinking. The article argues that without such criteria, leaders default to over-investing to avoid forfeiting what's already been spent. Setting kill criteria in advance transforms quitting from a reactive, emotionally fraught decision into a strategic, planned one that frees resources for more attainable goals.
points: Strategic quitting — deciding to walk away because the data says the goal is no longer attainable — is distinct from reactive, emotionally driven quitting.
Decision expert Annie Duke's "kill criteria" are checkpoints set before a project begins to signal when it's time to walk away.
Setting kill criteria in advance helps leaders avoid the sunk-cost fallacy that keeps them over-investing in failing efforts.
Strategic quitting frees resources and mental energy for goals that are actually attainable.
quotes: walking away from an unattainable goal is not a failure but a crucial leadership skill for organizational effectiveness.
